Applied Thermodynamics · Dr. Moustafa M. Amer · Midterm

Thermodynamics, from zero

You don't need any background. Start with the short explanation below, follow the one-day plan, and do one problem at a time. Every solution is written out step by step, so you can always check yourself.

Start hereSee the one-day planSteam tables (PDF)

10-minute read

Start from zero

A power plant turns heat into electricity. Fuel burns, the heat makes a turbine spin, and the turbine turns a generator. This course asks one question: how much of that heat becomes useful work? That share is the efficiency, η.

Machine 1 · Lectures 1–2

Steam plant (Rankine cycle)

Water goes round a loop of four parts:

  1. Pump: pushes the water to high pressure. It needs a little work.
  2. Boiler: heats the water into hot steam. This is the heat in.
  3. Turbine: the steam spins it. This is the work out.
  4. Condenser: cools the steam back to water. This is the heat thrown away.

Machine 2 · Lecture 3

Gas turbine (Brayton cycle)

The same idea with air instead of water:

  1. Compressor: squeezes the air.
  2. Burner: fuel heats the air.
  3. Turbine: the hot air spins it.
  4. The exhaust leaves to the atmosphere.

No tables needed here: only temperatures and two constants.

The only idea you need

Every part follows one rule: energy in − energy out = change in h. Here h (enthalpy) just means "energy carried by 1 kg of fluid". For steam you read it from the steam table. Applied to the four parts:

 pump wp=h2−h1
 boiler qin=h3−h2
 turbine wT=h3−h4
 condenser qout=h4−h1
 efficiency η=wT−wpqin

That's the whole course in five lines. Reheat, feedwater heaters and turbine efficiencies are the same loop with extra parts added.

How every exam answer is written (2 questions × 10 marks)

  1. Given: list the data.
  2. Find: what is asked.
  3. Draw the loop and the T-s diagram, and number the states 1, 2, 3, 4.
  4. State table: state | P | T | h | s | x.
  5. One equation per line: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser, η.
  6. Box the answers.
  7. Discussion table. It's required: without it you lose the question's marks. See the template.

Lecture 1 · Problem 1.1

Walkthrough: your first problem, explained line by line

The question. A steam power plant runs on the simple ideal Rankine cycle. Steam enters the turbine at 3 MPa and 350°C and is condensed at 75 kPa. Find the thermal efficiency.

Open the steam tables PDF next to this page and look up each value yourself as we go.

Step 0

Draw the loop and name the states

Always start here. The four states are the four places between the parts. Two pressures only: the boiler side (states 2 and 3) is at 3 MPa = 3000 kPa, and the condenser side (states 4 and 1) is at 75 kPa.

P2=P3=3000kPa( boiler side )P4=P1=75kPa( condenser side )

Step 1

State 1: water leaving the condenser

The condenser turns steam back into water completely, so state 1 is saturated liquid at 75 kPa. In the saturated-by-pressure table (Table 2), find the 75 kPa row and read hf and vf. The subscript f means "liquid".

h1=hfat75kPa=384.44kJ/kgv1=vfat75kPa=0.001037m³/kg

Step 2

Pump: from 1 to 2

The pump pushes liquid from 75 kPa to 3000 kPa. Liquid barely compresses, so the pump work is simply volume × pressure rise. Use kPa, so the answer comes out in kJ/kg. It is tiny, and that is normal.

wp=v1(P2−P1)=0.001037(3000−75)=3.03kJ/kgh2=h1+wp=384.44+3.03=387.47kJ/kg

Step 3

State 3: steam entering the turbine

Is 350°C above boiling at 3 MPa? Boiling at 3 MPa is 233.8°C (Table 2), so yes: the steam is superheated. Use the superheated table (Table 3), block "P = 3 MPa", row 350°C, and read h and s.

h3=3116.1kJ/kgs3=6.7449kJ/kg·K

Step 4

State 4: steam leaving the turbine

An ideal turbine does not change entropy, so s4 = s3. At 75 kPa, sg = 7.4557. Our s is smaller, so state 4 is a wet mixture, and we need its quality x (how much of it is vapour).

s4=s3=6.7449kJ/kg·Kx4=s4−sfsfg=6.7449−1.21326.2425=0.8861h4=hf+x4·hfg=384.44+0.8861(2277.9)=2403.0kJ/kg

Step 5

Energy of each part

Now just subtract enthalpies, using the five-line box.

wT=h3−h4=3116.1−2403.0=713.1kJ/kgqin=h3−h2=3116.1−387.47=2728.6kJ/kgqout=h4−h1=2403.0−384.44=2018.6kJ/kgwnet=wT−wp=713.1−3.03=710.1kJ/kg

Step 6

Efficiency

Useful work divided by the heat you paid for. Check: q_in − q_out must give the same w_net.

ηth=wnetqin=710.12728.6=0.2602=26.0% check =qin−qout=710.1kJ/kg✓

ηth=26.0%

Step 7

Discussion table (required in the exam)

Judge your own answer against normal values. This is what the TA described.

ResultMy valueNormal rangeWhy
ηth26.0%25–45%, below Carnot (41.4%)✓reasonable for a simple steam cycle
x40.886≥ 0.88✓dry enough for the turbine blades
rBW0.43%< 2%✓pumping liquid needs very little work

You've just done the most common exam question. Next: Must do 2 → (same steps, new numbers).

Reference · read once

The big picture and every symbol

Thermodynamics is the bookkeeping of energy. A power cycle is a machine that takes heat from something hot (burning fuel), turns part of it into shaft work (to spin a generator), and throws the rest away to something cold (a river or the air). The working fluid goes round and round, so it ends each lap in the state it started.

Two numbers tell you how good a cycle is: the net work it gives per kg of fluid, and the thermal efficiency η = (work out)/(heat in). The second law says η can never reach 100%; the best possible is the Carnot value 1 − T_low/T_high.

The course covers two families:

  • Vapour cycles (Rankine): water boils and condenses. These run coal, nuclear and gas steam power plants. Lectures 1–2.
  • Gas cycles (Brayton): air stays a gas. These run jet engines and gas-turbine power plants. Lecture 3.

Every steady-flow device uses the same energy balance

q − w = hout − hin (kJ/kg)

Pumps, turbines, boilers and condensers are just this equation with one term set to zero: pumps and turbines have no heat (q = 0), and boilers and condensers have no work (w = 0). That is the whole trick of the course.

Glossary: every symbol and unit

Ppressure. kPa (1 bar = 100 kPa, 1 MPa = 1000 kPa). Tables use absolute pressure.
Ttemperature. °C in steam tables; always K (= °C + 273.15) in Carnot and gas formulas.
vspecific volume, m³/kg (= 1/ρ). Liquid water ≈ 0.001 m³/kg.
hspecific enthalpy, kJ/kg: the energy carried per kg of flowing fluid. The main variable of every balance.
sspecific entropy, kJ/kg·K. Constant in an ideal (isentropic) pump or turbine: sin = sout.
xquality (dryness fraction) = mass of vapour / total mass, 0 (sat. liquid) to 1 (sat. vapour). Moisture = 1 − x.
f, g, fgsubscripts: f = saturated liquid, g = saturated vapour, fg = g − f (e.g. hfg = latent heat).
qin, qoutheat added (boiler) and rejected (condenser) per kg, kJ/kg. Always positive numbers here.
wT, wp, wCturbine work out, pump work in, compressor work in, kJ/kg.
wnetwT − wp (or − wC) = qin − qout.
ηththermal efficiency = wnet/qin = 1 − qout/qin.
ηT, ηP, ηCisentropic efficiencies. Turbine: actual/ideal work. Pump and compressor: ideal/actual work.
rBWback work ratio = wp/wT (or wC/wT). Steam ≈ 0.004; gas turbines 0.4–0.8.
RWwork ratio = wnet/wT.
SSCspecific steam consumption = 3600/wnet, kg/kWh.
HRheat rate = 3600/η kJ/kWh (or 3412/η Btu/kWh).
ṁmass flow, kg/s. Power = ṁ × (per-kg value): kW = kg/s × kJ/kg.
y, zfraction of steam bled from the turbine to a feedwater heater, per kg through the boiler.
rppressure ratio P₂/P₁ of a compressor.
γ (k)cp/cv; 1.4 for air. Exponent (γ − 1)/γ = 0.2857.
cpspecific heat at constant pressure; air 1.005 kJ/kg·K.
εregenerator effectiveness = actual/maximum heat transferred.
TTDterminal temperature difference of a closed FWH: bled-steam exit temperature − feedwater exit temperature.
kPa·m³/kgequals kJ/kg, so v·ΔP with P in kPa gives kJ/kg directly.

How to look things up

Using the steam tables

The doctor's steam table: open the PDF ("Properties of Water and Steam", NIST data, 104 pages). It has the same three tables as Dr. Hamed El-Tahan's booklet. Every table look-up in this guide now has a green "Doctor's table" note under it that names the table, the page and the row. Tap the page link to open the PDF at that page.

Mollier (h-s) chart: the doctor's table has no chart, so use this printable PDF (last pages) for the Lecture 2 chart readings.

The mark to look for

In every solution, under each table look-up, you will see a green box like this one. It means "this number comes from the doctor's table, and here is exactly where":

📖 Find it in the doctor's table Table 3 · page 69 (block p = 3 MPa), right half of the page, row T = 350°C: h = 3116.1, s = 6.7449

Read it as: open Table 3, go to page 69 (the page titled "p = 3.0 MPa"), look in the right half, find the row that starts with 350, and read h and s from it.

How the doctor's table is organised

TablePagesUse it when you know…What one row looks like
Table 1
saturated, by temperature		5–14a temperature, and the water is saturated (liquid, vapour or a mixture)T (°C) · psat (MPa) · vf vg · uf ug · hf hg hfg · sf sg sfg

Three traps in this table

  1. Pressures are in MPa. kPa ÷ 1000 = MPa, bar ÷ 10 = MPa. So 10 kPa = 0.010 MPa = 0.1 bar, and 30 bar = 3.0 MPa.
  2. Column order is hf, hg, hfg (and sf, sg, sfg). hg comes before hfg, unlike Çengel. Check: hf + hfg = hg.
  3. A Table 3 page is split into a left half and a right half. Read down the left half first, then carry on down the right half. The row at Tsat is printed twice: the first one is saturated liquid, the second is saturated vapour. Rows above it are subcooled (compressed) water. Rows below it are superheated steam.

How to read the steam tables in 4 questions

  1. Which region am I in? Look up Tsat at your pressure in Table 2. T < Tsat → compressed liquid (Table 3, rows above Tsat, or h ≈ hf at T). T = Tsat → mixture (you need x). T > Tsat → superheated (Table 3, rows below Tsat).
  2. Saturated liquid (pump inlet): Table 2, row at the condenser pressure. h₁ = hf, v₁ = vf.
  3. Mixture (turbine exit): Table 2, row at the exit pressure. If s < sg: x = (s − sf)/sfg, then h = hf + x·hfg. If s > sg, the exit is superheated, so go to the Table 3 page for that pressure and find the two rows whose s values bracket yours.
  4. Superheated (turbine inlet): Table 3, page for the pressure, row for the temperature: read h and s.

Worked example: one full Rankine look-up, page by page

Plant: boiler 3 MPa, turbine inlet 350°C, condenser 10 kPa (Lecture 1, Solved Problem 3.1(a)).

State 1, pump inlet (saturated liquid at 10 kPa): 10 kPa = 0.010 MPa. Table 2, page 16, row "0.010": Tsat = 45.806°C, vf = 0.00101027 m³/kg, hf = 191.81 kJ/kg.

State 3, turbine inlet (3 MPa, 350°C): Table 3, page 69 is titled "p = 3.0 MPa (Tsat = 233.853)". 350°C is above 233.853°C, so the steam is superheated. In the right half, row 350: h = 3116.1 kJ/kg, s = 6.7449 kJ/kg·K.

State 4, turbine exit (10 kPa, s = 6.7449): back to Table 2, page 16, row "0.010": sf = 0.64920, sg = 8.1488, sfg = 7.4996, hfg = 2392.1. Since 6.7449 < 8.1488 it is a mixture: x = (6.7449 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.8128, and h = 191.81 + 0.8128 × 2392.1 = 2136.1 kJ/kg.

Interpolation, written out

Example: 6 MPa and 550°C. Table 3, page 75 (p = 6.0 MPa) prints rows every 20°C up here, so 550°C falls between 540°C and 560°C.

540°C → h = 3517.7, s = 7.0020; 560°C → h = 3564.8, s = 7.0591. At 550°C: h = 3517.7 + (550 − 540)/(560 − 540) × (3564.8 − 3517.7) = 3541.3 kJ/kg; s = 7.0020 + (550 − 540)/(560 − 540) × (7.0591 − 7.0020) = 7.0306 kJ/kg·K

Rule: value = lower + (wanted − lower)/(upper − lower) × (upper value − lower value). Do it for h and for s separately. The doctor's table has many more rows than Çengel (every 10°C at mid temperatures), so you interpolate less often. Example: 8 MPa, 480°C is printed directly on page 79: h = 3349.6, s = 6.6613. When the pressure has no page of its own (e.g. 0.98 MPa or 12.5 MPa), interpolate inside the two neighbouring pages, then between them, or read the h-s chart as the doctor does.

Example: isentropic expansion to 0.7 MPa with s = 6.6000.

Table 2, page 18, row "0.70": sf = 1.9918, sg = 6.7071, sfg = 4.7153, hf = 697.00, hfg = 2065.8. s = 6.6000 < sg, so wet mixture: x = (6.6000 − 1.9918)/4.7153 = 0.9773; h = 697.00 + (0.9773)(2065.8) = 2715.9 kJ/kg

Where the guide's numbers come from

  • Lecture 1 and Sheets 2–3 quote Çengel's tables: A-4 = the doctor's Table 1, A-5 = Table 2, A-6 and A-7 = Table 3. Both come from the same IAPWS/NIST data, so the numbers match to the last digit. Every look-up in this guide was checked against the doctor's PDF.
  • Lecture 2 uses the doctor's Tables (1)–(3) plus the h-s (Mollier) chart for superheated states. Chart readings are rounded (3540, 2370 …), so differences of 5–10 kJ/kg from the table are normal and accepted.
  • Lecture 3 uses no steam tables: air with cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4 (Sheet 3's 9-121/122 use Çengel's air table A-17).

Using the h-s (Mollier) chart (Lecture 2)

  • Find the turbine inlet where the P line crosses the T line, and read h on the vertical axis.
  • Go straight down (s = const) to the exit pressure line, and read h. That is the isentropic exit.
  • For an actual turbine, compute h_a = h₁ − η_T(h₁ − h_s), then read x where that h meets the exit pressure line.

Pump work shortcut

w_p = v₁(P₂ − P₁) with P in kPa gives kJ/kg directly. Lecture 2 uses v ≈ 0.001 m³/kg; Lecture 1 and the sheets use v_f from the table. Both are accepted; use v_f when it is in your table.

Lecture 1 · part A

Carnot cycle and the ideal Rankine cycle

In plain words

A reversible process could be run backwards leaving no trace on the surroundings. Nothing real is reversible, because friction, fast expansion, mixing and heat transfer across a temperature difference all spoil it. Reversible processes are still the benchmark: a cycle made only of them (the Carnot cycle) has the highest possible efficiency between two temperatures.

The Carnot cycle has 4 reversible steps: isothermal heat in at T_H, isentropic expansion, isothermal heat out at T_L, and isentropic compression. Inside the steam dome, constant pressure means constant temperature, so a "Carnot vapour cycle" is a rectangle on the T-s diagram. It still fails in practice:

  • T_max is capped below the critical point (374°C, 22.06 MPa) if heat is to be added isothermally.
  • The turbine expands deep into the wet region; droplets erode the blades. x < 0.90 is not tolerated.
  • A compressor that pumps a liquid-vapour mixture (state 4 → 1) is impractical, and condensation would have to stop at exactly the right quality.

The Rankine cycle fixes this: superheat the steam (dry turbine exit) and condense it completely, so a simple pump handles pure liquid.

 Boiler 2→3qin=h3−h2
 Turbine 3→4wT,out=h3−h4

The doctor's steps for any Rankine problem

  1. Draw the component sketch and the T-s diagram and number the states 1–4.
  2. State 1: saturated liquid at the condenser pressure, so h₁ = h_f and v₁ = v_f.
  3. Pump: w_p = v₁(P₂ − P₁), h₂ = h₁ + w_p.
  4. State 3: superheated table at (P₃, T₃), giving h₃ and s₃.
  5. State 4: s₄ = s₃ at the condenser pressure, giving x₄ and h₄.
  6. Energy balances: q_in, q_out, w_T, w_net, η. Cross-check w_net = q_in − q_out.

Common traps

  • Using °C in 1 − T_L/T_H. Always convert to kelvin.
  • P in MPa inside v·ΔP: convert to kPa so the answer comes out in kJ/kg.
  • Forgetting that P₂ = P₃ (boiler pressure) and P₄ = P₁ (condenser pressure).
  • Reading h_g instead of the superheated h at the turbine inlet.
  • v·ΔP is only for liquids. Never use it for a turbine.

Lecture 1 · part B

Real cycles and three ways to raise efficiency

In plain words

Real plants lose to fluid friction (pressure drops in the boiler, condenser and pipes) and to heat loss. The pump and turbine are not isentropic: entropy grows, so the actual exit states move to the right on the T-s diagram. The pump needs more work than ideal and the turbine gives less. Condensate is slightly subcooled to avoid cavitation in the pump.

ηPwswa=h2s−h1h2a−h1→h2a=h1+h2s−h1ηP
ηTwaws=h3−h4ah3−h4s→h4a=h3−ηT(h3−h4s)
 typical ηP≈0.85,ηT≈0.87; ideal ratio is inverted so both stay ≤1
x4ah4a−hfhfgat the condenser pressure 

Diagrams (swipe)

heat added heat rejected work (isentropic) actual path

The governing principle

Raise the average temperature at which heat is added, or lower the average temperature at which heat is rejected.

LeverEffect on ηSide effect
Lower condenser pressure↑ (lower T of heat rejection)more moisture at turbine exit; air leaks into the condenser. Limit: T_sat must be at least ~10°C above the cooling water, e.g. a 15°C river needs T_sat ≥ 25°C, so P ≥ 3.2 kPa. That is why η is higher in winter.
Superheat to higher T↑, and w_net ↑exit drier (good); metals limit T ≈ 620°C
Raise boiler pressure↑ (higher T of boiling)exit wetter, which needs reheat. Supercritical plants run above 22.06 MPa: about 40% (fossil), 34% (nuclear).

Lecture 2 · part A

Rankine with tables and chart, and the reheat cycle

In plain words

Lecture 2 redoes the Rankine cycle with the doctor's own tables and the h-s chart, then adds reheat. High boiler pressure is good for η but makes the turbine exhaust too wet. The fix is to expand the steam in a high-pressure turbine, send it back to the boiler to be reheated (usually to the original temperature), then expand it in a low-pressure turbine.

  • One reheat adds about 4–5% to η. A second adds about half as much, and a third under 1%, so more than two is not worth the cost.
  • Optimum reheat pressure is about ¼ to ⅕ of the maximum cycle pressure.
  • Don't let the steam go deep into the wet region before reheating.
  • Disadvantages: high material cost and more heat rejected.
 Pump Q˙=0,W˙pump,in=m˙(h2−h1)
 Boiler W˙=0,Q˙boiler,in=m˙(h3−h2)
 Turbine Q˙=0,W˙turbine,out=m˙(h3−h4)
 Condenser W˙=0,Q˙cond,out=m˙(h4−h1)
qin( reheat )(h3−h2)+(h5−h4)
wT( reheat )(h3−h4)+(h5−h6)
η( reheat )[(h3−h4)+(h5−h6)−(h2−h1)][(h3−h2)+(h5−h4)]
h2( doctor )h1+0.001(P2−P1),Pin kPa 

Diagrams (swipe)

heat added heat rejected work (isentropic) actual path

Doctor's steps for reheat

  1. States 1, 2 as before.
  2. State 3 from (P_boiler, T₃); state 4 from (P_reheat, s₄ = s₃).
  3. State 5 from (P_reheat, T₅); state 6 from (P_cond, s₆ = s₅).
  4. If x₆ is given, use it first: s₆ = s_f + x₆s_fg = s₅. That fixes the unknown (reheat pressure or temperature).

Common traps

  • Forgetting the reheat term (h₅ − h₄) in q_in.
  • w_net = w_T − w_p, so w_T = w_net + w_p, not − (the slide makes this slip in Example 4).
  • Mass flow: kg/s × 3600 = kg/h.

Lecture 2 · part B

Regeneration: feedwater heaters

In plain words

The cold liquid leaving the pump enters the boiler far below the boiling temperature, so heat is added at a low average temperature, which is bad for η. Regeneration bleeds a little steam from the turbine (fraction y per kg) and uses it to pre-heat this feedwater. That steam gives up some turbine work, but the boiler now adds heat at a higher average temperature, so η rises. Modern plants use 5–8 heaters.

Open FWH (mixing chamber)Closed FWH (heat exchanger)
Howbled steam and feedwater mix; leaves as sat. liquid at heater pressurestreams don't mix; drain is pumped forward or trapped backward
Prossimple, cheap, best heat transfer; also deaerates (removes dissolved gases)one pump can serve several heaters; up to 7 in big plants
Conseach heater needs its own pump; usually only 1 usedcomplex, expensive, less efficient (no direct contact)

Advantages of regeneration: less boiler heat; higher η (higher average temperature of heat addition); lower thermal stresses in the boiler; smaller condenser. Disadvantages: less turbine work per kg; a more complex plant; more maintenance; heaters cost money and the η gain is modest.

 Open FWH balance y·h6+(1−y)·h2=1·h3→y=h3−h2h6−h2
wT( OFWH )(h5−h6)+(1−y)(h6−h7)
wp( OFWH )(1−y)(h2−h1)+(h4−h3)
qin,qouth5−h4;(1−y)(h7−h1)
 CFWH forward y·h7+(1−y)h2=y·h3+(1−y)h9; mixing :h5=y·h4+(1−y)h9
 CFWH backward y·h7+h2=y·h4+h3; trap :h5=h4;wp=h2−h1
 TTD T3−T9( bled-steam exit − feedwater exit ); TTD =0→T9=T3

Diagrams (swipe)

heat added heat rejected work (isentropic) actual path

Doctor's steps

  1. Mark mass fractions on the sketch: 1 kg through boiler, y bled, 1 − y to the condenser.
  2. Find every h (pumps first, then the turbine states, all with s = s_inlet).
  3. Energy balance on the heater gives y.
  4. Turbine work, pump work and q_out are weighted by the mass that actually flows there.

Common traps

  • Multiplying q_in by (1 − y). The full 1 kg goes through the boiler (unless steam is bled before a reheater).
  • In a closed FWH the feedwater is already at boiler pressure, so pump I lifts it to P_boiler, not to the bleed pressure.
  • In a reheat-regen plant bled before the reheater, only (1 − y) is reheated: q_in = (h₅ − h₄) + (1 − y)(h₇ − h₆).

ResultMy valueNormal rangeWhy
ηth36.7%25–45%( ideal reheat / regen up to ≈49%)✓below the Carnot limit of 50.9% and inside the normal range

In words: η = 36.7% is reasonable: it is below the Carnot limit (50.9%) and in the normal 25–45% range for steam plants. Exit quality x = 0.771 is below 0.88, which is too wet for the turbine blades; reheat or a higher turbine-inlet temperature would fix it.

Lecture 3 · part A

The Brayton (Joule) cycle

In plain words

A gas turbine sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it at constant pressure, expands the hot gas through a turbine, and throws the exhaust out. On paper we close the loop (the air-standard model): air is the working fluid, combustion becomes constant-pressure heat addition, and the exhaust becomes constant-pressure heat rejection. Four internally reversible steady-flow processes: 1-2 isentropic compression, 2-3 P = const heat in, 3-4 isentropic expansion, 4-1 P = const heat out.

Ideal-cycle efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio (and γ). The compressor eats a big share of the turbine work (back work ratio 0.4–0.8), which is why turbine and compressor efficiencies matter so much here.

Common traps

  • Temperatures in K for r_p^{(γ−1)/γ} formulas.
  • T₄ actual = T₃ − η_T(T₃ − T₄s) but T₂ actual = T₁ + (T₂s − T₁)/η_C. The efficiency goes on opposite sides.
  • w_net is a small difference of big numbers: keep 4 significant figures until the end.
  • Section 4: c_p = 1.108 and k = 1.35 are given, so use them, not 1.005/1.4.

Lecture 3 · part B

Regeneration, intercooling and reheating

In plain words

Gas-turbine exhaust is often hotter than the compressor exit. A regenerator (counter-flow heat exchanger) uses it to warm the compressed air before the burner, so less fuel is needed for the same work. It only works when T₄ > T₂, so it is most effective at low pressure ratios and low T_min/T_max.

Intercooling (compress in stages, cool between) cuts compressor work. Reheating (expand in stages, reheat between) raises turbine work. Both raise w_net but lower η unless a regenerator is added. With many stages plus regeneration the cycle approaches the Ericsson cycle, whose efficiency equals Carnot's. Best performance: equal stage pressure ratios, r_{p,stage} = √r_{p,total} for two stages, complete intercooling (T₃ = T₁) and complete reheating (T₈ = T₆).

εqregen,actqregen,max=h5−h2h4−h2≈T5−T2T4−T2
T5T2+ε(T4−T2)
qin( regen )cp(T3−T5)
η( ideal regen )1−(T1T3)·rp(γ−1)/γ

Lec 3 · Example 3

Two-stage compression and expansion, with/without regenerator

What it's about: Multi-stage gas turbine (advanced).

Ideal gas turbine with two compression stages (intercooling) and two expansion stages (reheat). Each stage pressure ratio is 3. Air enters each compressor stage at 300 K and each turbine stage at 1200 K.

Given

  • rp,st=3
  • T1=T3=300K
  • T6=T8=1200K
  • (b) regenerator ε=0.75

Find

back work ratio and ηth: (a) no regenerator, (b) with regenerator

Answer

rBW=0.342in both cases 

(a)η=38.2%

(b)η=55.7%

On-paper solution

3 · Energy balances, one line at a time

T2=T4=300(3)0.2857=410.6K T7=T9=120030.2857=876.7K wC=2cp(T2−T1)=2(1.005)(410.6−300)=222.35kJ/kg wT=2cp(T6−T7)=2(1.005)(1200−876.7)=649.79kJ/kg rBW=222.35649.79=0.342

(a) no regenerator

qin=cp(T6−T4)+cp(T8−T7)=1.005[(1200−410.6)+(1200−876.7)]=1118.2kJ/kg ηth=427.41118.2=38.2%

(b) with regenerator, ε = 0.75

T5=T4+ε(T9−T4)=410.6+0.75(876.7−410.6)=760.2K qin=1.005[(1200−760.2)+(1200−876.7)]=766.9kJ/kg ηth=427.4766.9=55.7%

rBW=0.342in both cases 

(a)η=38.2%

(b)η=55.7%

Exit quality x = 0.833 is below 0.88, which is too wet for the turbine blades; reheat or a higher turbine-inlet temperature would fix it. y = 0.145 is a small fraction of the flow, as expected for one heater.

Short answers

Theory quick-fire

What is a reversible process?

One that can be reversed leaving no trace on system or surroundings: net zero heat and work over the forward-plus-reverse process.

Name four irreversibilities.

Friction, unrestrained expansion, mixing of fluids, heat transfer across a finite ΔT (also electrical resistance, inelastic deformation, chemical reactions).

Internally vs externally reversible?

Internally: no irreversibilities inside the system boundary (quasi-equilibrium). Externally: none outside, i.e. heat crosses with infinitesimal dT.

Why can reversible heat transfer not be built?

Q = UAΔT. As ΔT → 0 the area (or time) needed goes to infinity.

Why is the Carnot vapour cycle impractical?

Two-phase compression is impractical; the turbine runs wet (erosion, x < 0.9); Tmax is capped below the critical point; condensation must stop at an exact quality.

What are the 4 processes of the ideal Rankine cycle?

1-2 isentropic compression (pump), 2-3 P = const heat addition (boiler), 3-4 isentropic expansion (turbine), 4-1 P = const heat rejection (condenser).

What areas on the T-s diagram mean what?

Under 2-3: qin. Under 4-1: qout. Enclosed area: wnet.

Why is the back work ratio of a steam cycle so small?

The pump moves liquid (tiny v), and w = ∫v dP, so wp ≈ 0.4% of wT. Gas compressors handle vapour-like gas, so 40–80%.

Three ways to raise Rankine efficiency?

Lower condenser pressure, superheat to higher T, raise boiler pressure. All raise the mean T of heat addition or lower the mean T of rejection.

Why is a plant more efficient in winter?

Colder cooling water allows a lower condenser saturation temperature, so lower pressure and lower heat-rejection temperature.

Why reheat?

To allow high boiler pressure without excessive turbine-exit moisture; it also raises the mean temperature of heat addition (≈ 4–5% per first reheat).

Why not more than two reheats?

Cost and complexity, metallurgical limits, diminishing returns (2nd ≈ half the 1st, 3rd < 1%), and a superheated exhaust raises qrej.

Why does regeneration raise η?

Feedwater enters the boiler hotter, so heat is added at a higher average temperature.

Open vs closed FWH?

Open: mixing, simple, cheap, deaerates, one pump each. Closed: no mixing, expensive, one pump serves several, up to 7 used.

What is deaeration?

Venting dissolved gases from the feedwater in the open FWH (gas solubility drops with temperature), which reduces corrosion.

Why is condensate subcooled in real plants?

To avoid cavitation (vapour bubbles collapsing) at the pump inlet.

What does η of an ideal Brayton cycle depend on?

Only the pressure ratio rp (and γ): η = 1 − 1/rp^{(γ−1)/γ}.

What limits Tmax and rp in gas turbines?

The turbine-blade material temperature.

Roles of air in a gas turbine?

Oxidant for combustion and coolant for components; air–fuel ratio 50 or more.

When is a regenerator useful?

Only when the turbine exhaust is hotter than the compressor exit; best at low pressure ratios.

Do intercooling and reheating raise η?

They raise wnet but lower η unless a regenerator is also used.

What is the Ericsson cycle?

Two isothermal and two isobaric processes with a regenerator. Its η equals Carnot. Many-stage intercool + reheat + regen Brayton approaches it.

Second-law efficiency?

ηII = ηth/ηth,rev; modern steam plants are 0.5–0.7.

Read before the exam

Exam format and the discussion table

There are no past exams in the folder, so this map is an estimate. It is built from how much each topic gets in the lectures, sections and sheets, and from the doctor's own rules.

What the class group says about the exam

  • 2 questions, 10 marks each, in the midterm and the final. The questions are the lecture and section problems, so re-solve those.
  • Always write a discussion, even if the question does not ask, as a small table at the end of your answer. No discussion means you lose the question's marks.
  • Discussion = judge your result. Example: "the highest η of a Rankine cycle is about 40–45%; my answer is lower, so it is correct". If it is wrong, say which value is off and why.
  • If the steps or result are wrong you only get the formula marks. Write in English, clearly, and keep it short.

Does Thermal-Fluid Science Lec 1 belong to this course? No. It is the doctor's other course (Thermal-Fluid Science, Çengel's Fundamentals of Thermal-Fluid Sciences; its guideline slide is even tagged "Computer Applications 3"). Its content (systems, properties, pressure, temperature) is first-year background that this course assumes. Know it well enough to read the cycle problems, but expect few or no exam marks from it. Its first slide is still useful: it states the doctor's exam rules, used in the next section.

Verification and mistakes found

56problems recomputed in code
42/42energy-balance & table checks pass
81/87answers within 0.6% of the slide/sheet
15errors in notes

How it was checked. A Python program solved every problem with IAPWS-95 steam properties (the formulation the printed tables come from) and the doctor's constant-c_p air model. It did all interpolations as a student would, and checked that every cycle closes: w_net computed from the work terms equals q_in − q_out, and every heater balance closes. Each answer was then compared with the slide or sheet.

Why my numbers sometimes differ slightly from the doctor's. (1) Lecture 2 reads h from the h-s chart (3540, 2370, …), which is good to about ±5–10 kJ/kg. (2) Lecture 2 uses v ≈ 0.001 m³/kg for pumps. (3) Some slides use an older table edition (h_f at 5 kPa = 137.82, now 137.75). (4) Rounding of intermediate values. None of these is a mistake. The list below only has real errors.

Every mistake found in the notes, sections and sheets

  1. Lec 2 · Reheat Example 3: The slides never compute part (a). With the slide's own chart numbers, η = 1532/3779 = 40.5%.
  2. Lec 2 · Reheat Example 4: Slide writes wt = wnet − wp = 1590 kJ/kg. Since wnet = wt − wp, the turbine work must be wnet + wp = 1610 kJ/kg. With the slide's chart values this gives h5 − h4 = 460 kJ/kg, qadd = 3657 kJ/kg and η = 43.7% (slide: 3637.35 kJ/kg and 44%).
  3. Lec 2 · OFWH Example 1: Slide writes h4 = 798.33 + 0.001(15000 − 1200) but prints 814. With v = 0.001 that line gives 812.13 kJ/kg; 814 needs vf = 0.001138 m³/kg at 1.2 MPa, which I use here.
  4. Lec 2 · CFWH Example 1: Slide's pump I line uses (300 − 5) kPa. In a closed heater the feedwater is already at boiler pressure, so pump I must lift it to 6000 kPa (as Example 2 does): h2 = 143.75, not 138.05 kJ/kg.
  5. Lec 2 · CFWH Example 1: Slide prints qadd = 2743.5 kJ/kg; h6 − h5 = 3300 − 565.48 = 2734.5 kJ/kg (digits swapped). η stays 42%.
  6. Lec 2 · Solved problems, Example 1: Slide: η = 1091/2958 = 36.67%. That division actually gives 36.88%.
  7. Lec 2 · Solved problems, Example 2: Slide: Wp = h2a − h1 = 4.44 kJ/kg, but 142.29 − 137.82 = 4.47 kJ/kg. The effect is negligible.
  8. Lec 2 · Solved problems, Example 3: Slide: h2 = 137.82 + 0.001(10000 − 5) = 138.82 kJ/kg. Correct: 137.82 + 9.995 = 147.82 kJ/kg (Wp ≈ 10 kJ/kg, not 1). This changes Wnet to 1675 kJ/kg, ṁ to 29.85 kg/s and ṁcw to about 975 kg/s.
  9. Lec 2 · Solved problems, Example 4: Slide: wt = (3240 − 2635) + (3475 − 2320) = 1757 kJ/kg, but that sum is 1760 kJ/kg.
  10. Lec 2 · Solved problems, Example 4: Slide: η = 44.8%. With the slide's own numbers, qadd = (3240 − 157.9) + (3475 − 2635) = 3922 kJ/kg and η = 1737/3922 = 44.3%.
  11. Lec 2 · Solved problems, Example 4: Part (c), specific steam consumption, is asked but never answered on the slides: SSC = 3600/1737 = 2.07 kg/kWh.
  12. Lec 3 · Regeneration Example 1: Slide: wt = 1.005(1150 − 748) = 405.6 kJ/kg. In fact 1.005 × 402 = 404.0 kJ/kg, so wnet = 95.3 kJ/kg (not 97.0) and η = 21.2% (not 21.6%).
  13. Section 2 · Sheet 1, problem 28 (≈ Çengel 10-24): The section writes ṁf = 343.3 kJ/kg; the unit should be kg/s.
  14. Sheet 2 · 10-49: Sheet typo: 'h3 = hf @ 0.3 MPa = 670.38' should read @ 0.6 MPa (670.38 is the 0.6 MPa value). It also says y = ṁ10/ṁ5 where it means ṁ9/ṁ5.
  15. Section 4 · Q&A (Çengel 9-95): The solution sheet prints cp as 0.821 kJ/kg·K in the work lines, but its numbers were computed with 1.108. Use cp = 1.108; cv is not needed. It also prints the heat input as '17,47 kW' (should be 17,147 kW), labels the solution 9-88 although the problem is 9-95, and says 'variable specific heats' while using constant ones.
  16. Lec 3 · Assignment (Brayton regeneration): answer (a) 152.5 kJ/kg could not be reproduced with the doctor's method (114.1 kJ/kg); efficiency 36.0% agrees.
  17. Lec 1, Carnot slide: 41.5% (uses 273 K offset); with 273.15 it is 41.4%. Not really an error.
